text: Identities. (I1) For \(x\in Q\) the maps \(a\mapsto[a,x]\) and \(a\mapsto[x,a]\) are homomorphisms \(\gamma_2\to\gamma_3\); for instance \([ab,x]=[a,x]^b[b,x]=[a,x][b,x]\), as \([[a,x],b]\in[\gamma_3,\gamma_2]=1\). (I2) The pairings \(\gamma_3\times Q\to\gamma_4\), \((c,x)\mapsto[c,x]\), and \(\gamma_2\times\gamma_2\to\gamma_4\) are bilinear. By (H1) the first one vanishes on \(\gamma_3^3\gamma_4\) and on cubes \(x^3\), and the second one on \(\gamma_2^3\gamma_3\). (I3) \(a\mapsto a^3\) is an endomorphism of \(\gamma_2\): \((ab)^3=a^3b^3[b,a]^3=a^3b^3\), as \([b,a]\in\gamma_4\) is central and of order dividing \(3\). Hence so is \(a\mapsto a^9\); as \(\gamma_2\) is generated by the commutators \([x,y]\), (H2) is equivalent to \([x,y]^9\in\gamma_4\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). (I4) \([x^3,a]=[x,a]^3=[x,a^3]\) and \([a,x^3]=[a,x]^3\) for \(x\in Q\), \(a\in\gamma_2\). This is identity (iii) of the proof of Theorem 6.6, whose proof uses only (H1) and \([\gamma_2,\gamma_3]=1\): for \(c=[x,a]\in\gamma_3\), \([x^3,a]=c^{x^2}c^xc=c^3[c,x]^3=c^3\), as \([c,x,x]\in\gamma_5=1\) and \([c,x]^3=1\). (I5) For \(X,y\in Q\) and \(c=[X,y]\), \([X^3,y]=c^{X^2}c^Xc=c^3[c,X]^3[c,X,X]\), since \([c,X]\in\gamma_3\) commutes with \(c\) and \([c,X,X]\in\gamma_4\) is central. (I6) Assume only (H1) and that \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) has exponent dividing \(9\). Then, for \(x,y\in Q\) and \(a\in\gamma_2\), \[[x^3,y]^3=[x^9,y]=[x,y]^9\,\bigl[[x,y]^9,x\bigr],\qquad [a,x^9]=[a,x]^9=[a^9,x],\qquad [x^{27},y]=[x,y]^{27}.\] Indeed, let \(c=[x,y]\) and \(d=[x^3,y]=c^3[c,x]^3[c,x,x]\) by (I5). Then \(d^3=c^9[c,x]^9=c^9[c^9,x]\) by (I1). For \(X=x^3\), (I4) gives \([d,X]=[d,x]^3\), so \([d,X]^3=[d^9,x]\) by (I1); here \(d\equiv c^3\pmod{\gamma_3}\) and \(c^9\in\gamma_3\), so \(d^9\in\gamma_3^3\) by (I3), and \([d^9,x]=1\) by (I2). Also \([d,X,X]=1\) by (I2), and (I5) gives \([x^9,y]=d^3\). Next, \([a,x^9]=[a,x^3]^3=[a,x]^9=[a^9,x]\) by (I4) and (I1). Finally, \(c'=[x^9,y]\) lies in \(\gamma_3\), so \([c',x^9]=1\) by (I2), and (I5) with \(X=x^9\) gives \([x^{27},y]=c'^3=c^{27}\), as \([c^9,x]\in\gamma_4\). Under (H2), \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) has exponent dividing \(9\), and \([x,y]^9\) and \(a^9\) lie in \(\gamma_4\), so they are central. Hence \[[x^3,y]^3=[x^9,y]=[x,y]^9\in\gamma_4,\qquad [x,y^9]=[x,y]^9,\qquad [a,x^9]=1,\] \[[x^{27},y]=[x,y^{27}]=1,\qquad \gamma_3^9=1;\] the last because \(\gamma_3\) is abelian and generated by the \([a,x]\), with \([a,x]^9=[a^9,x]=1\). Conversely, under (H1), if \([x^9,y]\in\gamma_4\) for all \(x,y\), then \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) has exponent dividing \(9\), as \([x^9,y]\equiv[x,y]^9\pmod{\gamma_3}\), and the first formula of (I6) gives \([x,y]^9\in\gamma_4\); this proves the equivalence stated after the theorem. (I7) For \(x\in Q\) with \(x^3\in\gamma_2\) and \(a\in\gamma_2\), \((xa)^3\equiv x^3a^3\pmod{\gamma_3}\), and for \(x,y\in Q\) with \(x^3,y^3\in\gamma_2\), \((xy)^3\equiv x^3y^3\pmod{\gamma_2^3\gamma_3}\) (Hall–Petrescu). So, on \(V=\{\bar x\in Q_{ab}:3\bar x=0\}\), the cube map induces a well-defined linear map \(\bar P\colon V\to L_2/3L_2\), \(\bar x\mapsto x^3\gamma_2^3\gamma_3\).

text: Claim: \(V\) has a basis \(z_1,\dots,z_s\) such that every \(V_j\), every \(V_j\cap K\) and every \(V_j\cap K'\) is spanned by a subset of it. By downward induction on \(j\), as in the proof of Theorem 6.9, let \(B_{j+1}\) be a basis of \(V_{j+1}\) such that \(B_{j+1}\cap K\) and \(B_{j+1}\cap K'\) are bases of \(V_{j+1}\cap K\) and \(V_{j+1}\cap K'\). Complete \(B_{j+1}\cap K\) by a set \(C_1\subset V_j\cap K\) to a basis of \(V_j\cap K\); then complete \((B_{j+1}\cap K')\cup C_1\) by a set \(C_2\subset V_j\cap K'\) to a basis of \(V_j\cap K'\); finally complete \(B_{j+1}\cup C_1\cup C_2\) by a set \(D\) to a basis \(B_j\) of \(V_j\). Each step is possible. First, \(\langle C_1\rangle\cap V_{j+1}\subseteq V_{j+1}\cap K=\langle B_{j+1}\cap K\rangle\), which meets \(\langle C_1\rangle\) trivially, so \(B_{j+1}\cup C_1\) is linearly independent. Second, \(\langle B_{j+1}\cup C_1\rangle\cap K'=\langle(B_{j+1}\cap K')\cup C_1\rangle\): if \(b+c\in K'\) with \(b\in V_{j+1}\) and \(c\in\langle C_1\rangle\subseteq K'\), then \(b\in V_{j+1}\cap K'=\langle B_{j+1}\cap K'\rangle\); so \(B_{j+1}\cup C_1\cup C_2\) is linearly independent. No element of \(C_2\) lies in \(K\) and no element of \(D\) lies in \(K'\), since otherwise independence would fail; so \(B_j\cap K\) and \(B_j\cap K'\) are bases of \(V_j\cap K\) and \(V_j\cap K'\). The basis \(B_0\) proves the claim.

text: As in the proof of Theorem 6.9, for \(z_i\in V_j\setminus V_{j+1}\) put \(d(i)=3^{j+1}\) and choose \(x_i\in Q\) with \((d(i)/3)\bar x_i=z_i\), numbered so that \(d(1)\le\dots\le d(s)\); then \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) is a basis of uniqueness of \(Q_{ab}\) with orders \(d(i)\). Put \(Y_i=x_i^{d(i)}\), so that \(Y_i\gamma_2^3\gamma_3=\bar P(z_i)\), and let \[N=\{i:z_i\in K\},\qquad A_W=\{i:z_i\in K'\setminus K\},\qquad A_9=\{i:z_i\notin K'\},\qquad A=A_W\cup A_9;\] (the index \(9\) of \(A_9\) refers to the order of \(\bar Y_i\) in \(L_2\), not to \(d(i)\)); let \(A_3=\{i\in A:d(i)=3\}\), \(N_3=\{i\in N:d(i)=3\}\) and \(N_9=\{i\in N:d(i)=9\}\). By the claim, the classes \(\bar P(z_i)\), \(i\in A_W\), are linearly independent in \(W\), and the classes \(\bar P(z_i)\), \(i\in A_9\), are linearly independent modulo \(W\). For \(d(i)=3\), replacing \(x_i\) by \(x_ia\) with \(a\in\gamma_2\) does not change \(\bar x_i\) and adds \(3\bar a\) to \(\bar Y_i\), by (I7). So we may assume that \(Y_i\in\gamma_3\) for \(i\in N_3\) and \(\bar Y_i\in L_2[3]\) for \(i\in A_3\cap A_W\).

text: A basis of \(L_2\). Of order \(3\): the \(\bar Y_h\) with \(h\in A_3\cap A_W\); elements \(\omega_h\in L_2[3]\) representing the classes \(\bar P(z_h)\), for \(h\in A_W\) with \(d(h)\ge9\); and elements of \(L_2[3]\) completing these to a basis of \(W\). Of order \(9\): the \(\bar Y_h\) with \(h\in A_9\), and elements completing their classes to a basis of \((L_2/3L_2)/W\). The classes of all these elements form a basis of \(L_2/3L_2\), so they generate \(L_2\). Those of the second kind have order \(9\), as they do not lie in \(L_2[3]+3L_2\) and \(L_2\) has exponent dividing \(9\) by (H2); there are \(\dim W\) of the first kind, and \(\dim W\) is the number of cyclic factors \(C_3\) of \(L_2\). So the product of their orders is \(|L_2|\), and they form a basis of uniqueness of \(L_2\), with orders \(e(k)\in\{3,9\}\); we number it so that the orders do not decrease. Let \(x_{2\sigma(h)}\) be the element corresponding to \(h\in A\) (that is, \(\bar Y_h\) or \(\omega_h\)). Then \(x_{2\sigma(h)}\equiv Y_h\pmod{\gamma_2^3\gamma_3}\) for all \(h\in A\), and for the constants \(b_{ik}\) of \(Y_i\equiv\prod_kx_{2k}^{b_{ik}}\pmod{\gamma_3}\) we have \(b_{i\cdot}\equiv\delta_{\sigma(i),\cdot}\pmod3\) for \(i\in A\) and \(b_{i\cdot}\equiv0\pmod3\) for \(i\in N\); exactly, \(b_{i\cdot}=\delta_{\sigma(i),\cdot}\) for \(i\in A_3\) and \(b_{i\cdot}=0\) for \(i\in N_3\). For \(d(i)\ge9\) there may be additional terms \(3b'_{ik}\) in the columns \(k\) of order \(9\). Let \(x_{31},\dots\) be a basis of uniqueness of \(L_3\); its orders \(f(l)\) divide \(9\), as \(\gamma_3^9=1\). As in the proofs of Theorems 6.6 and 6.9, \(x_{2k}^{e(k)}\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{d_{kl}}\), \(Y_h\equiv\prod_kx_{2k}^{b_{hk}}\cdot\bar y_h\) with \(\bar y_h=\prod_lx_{3l}^{c_{hl}}\), and \([Y_g,x_h]\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{\alpha^{(gh)}_l}\), all modulo \(\gamma_4\).

text: Tahara's conditions. By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1], \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \(g\) of the proof of Theorem 6.9, with the present \(Y_i=x_i^{d(i)}\) and \(q_{ij}=d(j)/d(i)\), over the integer families satisfying (A)–(F). Now (D) holds modulo \((d(i),e(k))\), (E) modulo \((d(i),f(l))\) and (F) modulo \(e(k)\), all in \(\{3,9\}\); we use them only modulo \(3\). Condition (B) is an equation in \(\mathbb{Z}\): \[\textstyle\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}b_{hk}+d(i)v_{ik}+e(k)v'_{ik}=0,\] and (E) reads \[\textstyle\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}c_{hl}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}\bigl(\alpha^{(hi)}_l+c_{hl}\bigr)-E^w_{il}\pmod{(d(i),f(l))},\] \[\textstyle E^w_{il}=\sum_{g\le i\le h}w_{gih}\alpha^{(gh)}_l+\sum_{g\le h\le i}w_{ghi}\alpha^{(gh)}_l+\sum_{i<g\le h}w'_{igh}\alpha^{(gh)}_l,\] whose distinguished index is \(g\) in each sum (the first, the first and the middle one respectively; \(w''\) does not occur in (E)). As in the proof of Theorem 6.9, modulo \(3\): (c1) \(3\mid u_{ij}\) if \(i<j\) and \(d(i)=d(j)\), by (C). (c2) \(3\mid u_{ih}\) if \(h\in A\) and \(i<h\): (B) for the column \(\sigma(h)\) modulo \(3\), since \(b_{h'\sigma(h)}\equiv\delta_{h'h}\) and \(3\) divides \(d(i)\) and \(e(k)\). (c3) Every coefficient \(w,w',w''\) whose distinguished index lies in \(A\) is divisible by \(3\): (D) for the column \(\sigma(h)\) modulo \(3\). (c4) For \(h\in A\), \(v_{hk}\equiv0\) if \(k\notin\sigma(A)\), and \(V_{ih}:=v_{i\sigma(h)}\) (\(i,h\in A\)) is skew-symmetric modulo \(3\) with zero diagonal: (F) modulo \(3\). (c5) \(\alpha^{(gh)}=0\) if \(g\in N_3\), as \(Y_g\in\gamma_3\), or if \(d(g)\ge9\), as then \([Y_g,x_h]\in\gamma_4\) by (I6).

text: The rows (B) and (E) together. For a row \(i\) put \(\beta_{ik}=\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}b_{hk}\), \(R_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{v_{ik}}\) and \[Z_i=\prod_{h>i}Y_h^{-u_{ih}}\prod_{h<i}Y_h^{u_{hi}q_{hi}}\in\gamma_2.\] The left side of (E) is the coordinate vector of \(a_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{e(k)v'_{ik}}\in\gamma_3\) (for \(e(k)=3\) this is the cube of the \(a_i\) of the proof of Theorem 6.9), and \(e(k)v'_{ik}=-d(i)v_{ik}-\beta_{ik}\) by (B). As \(\gamma_2/\gamma_4\) is abelian and \(\prod_kx_{2k}^{b_{hk}}\equiv Y_h\bar y_h^{-1}\pmod{\gamma_4}\), \[a_i\equiv R_i^{-d(i)}\,Z_i\,\prod_{h>i}\bar y_h^{u_{ih}}\prod_{h<i}\bar y_h^{-u_{hi}q_{hi}}\pmod{\gamma_4}.\] So the terms with \(c_{hl}\) in (E) cancel exactly against the \(\bar y_h\), and (E) for the row \(i\) is equivalent to \[R_i^{-d(i)}Z_i\equiv-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}\,\alpha^{(hi)}-E^w_i\quad\text{in }L_3,\ \text{coordinatewise modulo }(d(i),f(l)).\tag{$\ast$}\] Here \(R_i^{-d(i)}Z_i\in\gamma_3\), as \(a_i\) and the \(\bar y_h\) lie in \(\gamma_3\). Neither the elementarity of \(L_2\) nor \(\pi\) is needed for this; in the proof of Theorem 6.9 the same step was made through \(\pi(a_i)\).

If \(d(i)=d(j)=3\), then \(u_{ij}=3u'_{ij}\) by (c1) and \(3[Y_i,x_j]=[Y_i,x_j^3]=[Y_i,Y_j]\) by (I4); this vanishes if \(i\) or \(j\) lies in \(N_3\), as \([\gamma_3,\gamma_2]=1\).
